problem: The piston balance is stated as gas pressure = piston weight ÷ area. This omits the atmosphere pressing on the outside of the piston, so a student who uses this formula will get the wrong gas pressure for every usual cylinder problem.
fix: Write the balance as p_gas × A = W_piston + p_atm × A, i.e. p_gas = W_piston/A + p_atm, where W_piston is the piston weight in N, A is the piston area in m² and p_atm is the outside atmospheric pressure in kPa. Only if the outside of the piston is in vacuum does p_gas equal W_piston/A.

problem: The formula pV = C is placed immediately after the definition of a quasi-static process, which makes it look like a property that every quasi-static process obeys. It is not. pV = constant is one particular path (an isothermal path for an ideal gas, or simply the path assumed in the worked example). A general quasi-static path has no such relation.
fix: Say: 'A quasi-static process can follow any path; here is the path used in the worked example. If the product pV stays constant, then pV = C, where p is the absolute pressure in kPa, V is the volume in m³ and C is a constant in kPa·m³ = kJ. On a p–V diagram this particular path is a hyperbola.'

problem: Section 3 says a fast expansion is 'not at a state at all', while the trap says a fast process 'still passes through states, just not equilibrium states'. The two statements contradict each other and a student will not know which to write in the exam.
fix: Use one consistent line in both places: 'A fast process passes through non-equilibrium conditions, where p and T differ from point to point. These are not equilibrium states, so they have no single p or V and cannot be plotted as points on a p–V diagram.'

problem: The symbol dp is used without definition, and 'remove the imbalance' is misleading: adding a grain of sand or lowering the outside pressure creates a small imbalance to drive the change, it does not remove one.
fix: Write: 'Create a driving force that is infinitesimal — add one grain of sand to the piston, or lower the outside pressure by a tiny amount dp (a small change in pressure, in kPa).'

problem: The two examples move the system in opposite directions: adding sand to the piston compresses the gas, while lowering the outside pressure expands it. Placed side by side without comment, this reads as if both do the same thing.
fix: Label them: 'add one grain of sand to the piston (a small compression), or lower the outside pressure by dp (a small expansion).'

problem: The chapter never says that a truly quasi-static process takes infinite time, so students may conclude that any 'slow enough' real process is exactly quasi-static instead of only an approximation to it.
fix: Add one sentence: 'Infinite steps take infinite time, so no real process is exactly quasi-static; a slow real process is only a good approximation to it.'
